chapters.title: Chapter 6: Markets at Work and in Your Pocket

lessons.title: Case Study: Tracing One RBI Rate Hike Through Markets, a Company and Its Employees

children.text: Everything in this course now gets applied to one company and one decision. Six people in Mumbai raise the repo rate by half a percentage point. We will follow that single move through bond yields, the rupee, a factory in Nashik, a quarterly result, a share price, a set of ESOPs and finally a home loan EMI. Every number below reconciles, so you can check the chain yourself.

Suryodaya Appliances is a fictional listed maker of refrigerators and washing machines, based in Nashik, with 1,800 employees. It sells through 4,000 dealers, most of whom stock inventory using bank and NBFC credit. It imports compressors worth USD 15 million a year. It has ₹200 crore of floating rate bank debt. Around 200 managers hold ESOPs with an exercise price of ₹150.

stats.label: Revenue
stats.context: Operating profit of ₹120 crore, a 10% margin

stats.label: Floating Rate Debt
stats.context: At 9.0%, costing ₹18 crore of interest a year

stats.label: Earnings per Share
stats.context: ₹76.5 crore profit after tax, across 10 crore shares

body.text: The rate hike costs this company ₹1 crore in extra interest. It costs them about ₹14 crore in lost profit from customers who could no longer finance a purchase. The indirect channel is more than ten times the direct one, and almost nobody budgets for it.

body.title: From the MPC Statement to a Nashik Payslip

events.title: The MPC Hikes by 0.50 Points
events.description: Inflation has been above the tolerance band for two quarters. The committee raises the repo rate and keeps its stance tight, signalling that more may follow.

events.title: Bond Yields Jump
events.description: Government bond yields rise within minutes, as traders reprice. Corporate bond yields follow, since they are quoted as a spread over government paper. Nothing has happened in any factory yet.

events.title: Foreign Investors Reassess
events.description: With Indian rates higher, some global funds rebalance. Equity markets fall broadly, and Suryodaya's stock drops 3% along with its sector, despite no company-specific news.

events.title: The Rupee Weakens
events.description: Global dollar strength and foreign outflows push the rupee from ₹83 to ₹86 per dollar. Suryodaya's unhedged compressor imports now cost ₹3 more per dollar.

events.title: Dealer Financing Tightens
events.description: Dealers funding inventory on floating rate credit face higher costs and reduce stocking. Consumers buying appliances on EMI postpone purchases. Volumes fall about 4%.

events.title: The Company's Own Loan Reprices
events.description: At its contractual reset, the ₹200 crore facility moves from 9.0% to 9.5%, adding ₹1 crore to the annual interest bill.

events.title: Results, and a De-Rating
events.description: Profit falls. Management guides cautiously on demand. The market not only marks down earnings, it marks down the multiple it will pay for them.

events.title: It Reaches the Employees
events.description: ESOPs lose most of their value, the planned capacity expansion is deferred, hiring slows, and the same employees are separately paying higher EMIs on their own home loans.

body.caption: What Happened to ₹120 Crore of Operating Profit

cells: Revenue down 4%, at a 30% contribution margin
USD 15 million at ₹3 more per dollar
What the market would bear without losing more volume

body.title: Which Channel Did the Damage (₹ crore impact on operating profit)

body.label: The Lesson of That Chart
body.context: Most managers assume a rate hike reaches a company through its loan. In fact the largest hit came through customers who could no longer finance a purchase, and the second largest through the currency. The interest bill was the smallest of the three.

body.title: Check the Import Line Yourself
body.prompt: Suryodaya imports compressors worth USD 15 million a year. The rupee weakens from ₹83 to ₹86 per dollar. What is the extra annual cost, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: USD 15 million × ₹3 per dollar = ₹4.5 crore. Note that nobody in procurement negotiated worse terms and no supplier raised prices. A hedge booked before the move would have removed this line entirely, which is exactly the argument the treasury team had been making for two years.

children.text: From Profit to Share Price, and Why the Fall Is Bigger

Earnings per share fell about 14%, from ₹7.65 to ₹6.61. The share price fell about 25%. The gap is the multiple, which compressed from 30 to 26 as investors lowered what they would pay for a business now facing slower demand and higher rates. This is the two-engine framework from the previous chapter, operating on a real set of numbers.

stats.label: Share Price
stats.context: A fall of about 25%, because both engines moved together

stats.label: Market Capitalisation
stats.context: About ₹577 crore of shareholder value, with no cash leaving the company

body.title: Where Did Most of the Damage Come From?
body.question: Looking at the full chain, which single factor cost Suryodaya the most operating profit?
options: The ₹1 crore increase in its own interest cost
The ₹4.5 crore increase in import costs from the weaker rupee
The roughly ₹14.4 crore of lost profit from weaker demand as customer financing got costlier
The compression in its P/E multiple
body.explanation: Demand did the most damage by a wide margin. The multiple compression hurt shareholders but is not an operating cost at all, which is why it does not appear in the profit bridge. The practical implication is that a company with no debt whatsoever would still have been hit hard by this rate hike, through its customers.

stats.label: Fall in ESOP Value
stats.context: A 25% share price fall becomes a 73% fall in option value

stats.label: Employee Home Loan
stats.context: On a ₹50 lakh, 20-year loan moving from 8.5% to 9.0%

body.text: That 73% figure deserves attention from anyone holding options. Because an option only captures value above the exercise price, a moderate fall in the share price produces a dramatic fall in option value. The closer the share price sits to your exercise price, the more violent this effect. This is the arithmetic behind why ESOPs feel far more volatile than the stock itself.

body.title: What Management Controlled, and What It Did Not

columns.label: Within Their Control
points: Whether the compressor imports were hedged
Whether customer contracts allowed price revision
The mix of floating and fixed rate debt, and the reset structure
How much of the cost increase to pass on, and when
How clearly the situation was explained to employees and investors

columns.label: Entirely Outside It
points: Global fund allocation decisions affecting the share price
Whether consumers felt confident enough to buy on EMI
The multiple the market chose to pay for the same earnings

body.title: What Suryodaya Could Have Done Differently

children.text: None of these would have prevented the hike. Each would have reduced the damage:
A rolling forward cover on a predictable USD 15 million annual requirement would have fixed the compressor cost. This was the cheapest available fix and was never approved.
Fix part of the debt. ₹1 crore.
Splitting the ₹200 crore between floating and fixed rate borrowing would have halved the interest impact, at the cost of giving up some benefit had rates fallen instead.
Diversify dealer financing. Most of ₹14.4 crore.

Arranging channel financing tie-ups, or a subvention scheme during tight credit periods, would have kept dealers stocking. This was the largest loss and the one nobody treated as a financial market problem at all.
Being able to pass on input cost increases contractually, rather than negotiating each time, would have lifted the ₹6 crore recovery.

Explaining to employees and investors that the quarter was hit by transmission from a policy decision, with the bridge laid out line by line, does not change the profit. It changes whether people conclude that management lost control.

body.title: Your Turn: Write the Town Hall Explanation
body.scenario: You work in internal communications at Suryodaya. Profit after tax is down 14%, the share price is down 25%, ESOP value is down about 73%, the new line has been deferred, and increments will be modest. The CEO asks you for a five-minute town hall explanation that is honest, does not blame employees, and does not pretend everything is fine. Several employees have already asked whether the company is in trouble.
body.prompt: What do you say, in what order, and what do you deliberately avoid?
body.modelAnswer: Open with the cause, not the outcome, because people who do not understand why are left to invent a reason, and the reason they invent is usually that management failed. Say plainly that a policy rate increase, aimed at controlling inflation, reached the company through three channels: customers found it harder to finance purchases, so volumes fell about 4%; the rupee weakened, adding ₹4.5 crore to imported compressor costs; and the company's own loan repriced, adding ₹1 crore of interest. Show the bridge from ₹120 crore to ₹107 crore of operating profit, because a specific number is believed in a way that a general statement about headwinds is not. Then answer the question people are actually asking, which is whether the company is in trouble: profit fell, it did not disappear, the business remains profitable, there is no default risk on ₹200 crore of debt against ₹107 crore of operating profit, and no cash left the company because of the share price fall, since that was value transferred between investors. Third, be straight about consequences rather than burying them: the capacity expansion is deferred until the return clears the higher cost of capital, increments are tighter, and ESOP value has fallen sharply because options only capture value above the exercise price, which magnifies any share price move. Explain that arithmetic rather than letting people discover it alone. Fourth, say what the company is doing: hedging the import exposure, reviewing the fixed and floating debt mix, and working on dealer financing, which is where most of the loss occurred. Then close on what employees can and cannot control, crediting the operational execution that genuinely held up. Deliberately avoid four things: blaming employees or the sales team for a demand shock they did not cause; predicting where rates, the rupee or the share price will go next; telling anyone what to do with their ESOPs or shares, which is a personal decision and possibly restricted by the trading window in any case; and the phrase that everything is fine, because people can read a 25% price fall and will stop believing anything else you say. End by telling them where to get answers: compliance for anything about trading in company shares, HR for compensation questions, and the published results and investor presentation for the numbers themselves.

body.title: Run This Analysis on Your Own Employer
steps: Find out how much floating rate debt your company carries, and when it resets
Identify whether your customers buy using credit, since that is usually the largest and least monitored channel
List your company's foreign currency inflows and outflows, and ask whether they are hedged
Check whether customer contracts allow price revision when input costs rise
Work out your own concentration: salary, bonus, ESOPs and any employer shares, as a share of your total finances
Find your home loan's benchmark and reset date, so a policy change does not surprise you
Read your company's next quarterly result and try to build this same bridge yourself, from revenue down to profit

body.title: The Whole Course in Twelve Terms

cards.definition: In the primary market the issuer receives money. In the secondary market investors trade with each other and the company receives nothing.
The process by which a market sets a reference price for money, risk and ownership that the rest of the economy uses.
Share price times shares outstanding: the number to compare across companies, never the share price alone.
What the market pays per rupee of annual profit. It moves far faster than profits do.
The return a bond gives at its current price. It moves inversely to the price, so rising yields mean falling prices.
What banks pay to borrow from RBI, and the anchor for every other interest rate in the economy.
How a policy rate change reaches bond yields in minutes, loan rates in a quarter, and business decisions over several quarters.
An opinion on the likelihood of timely repayment. BBB minus is the investment grade floor that decides who may lend.
A weaker rupee, quoted as a higher number of rupees per dollar. It helps exporters and hurts importers.
Offsetting a real exposure to buy certainty. A position larger than the exposure is a trade, not a hedge.
Unpublished price sensitive information. Possession plus a trade, by you or someone you told, is the offence.
Salary, bonus, job security and savings all depending on one company, which is the largest financial risk most employees carry.

points: One policy decision reached this company through demand, the currency and its own interest cost, in that order of size
The largest hit, about ₹14.4 crore, came through customers who could no longer finance purchases, not through the company's loan
A debt-free company would still have been damaged by this rate hike, through its customers and its imports
Profit after tax fell about 14% while the share price fell about 25%, because earnings and the multiple moved together
A 25% share price fall cut ESOP value by about 73%, because options only capture value above the exercise price
Hedging the imports and fixing part of the debt were cheap, available and unapproved, which is the most common finding in cases like this
Every department experienced the same decision and most would have blamed something else, which is exactly what understanding markets prevents
You cannot forecast the next move, but you can now trace how any move will reach your company, your team and your own finances

body.text: Financial markets are not a spectator sport happening somewhere in Mumbai. They are the pricing system your salary, your savings, your employer's plans and your home loan all sit inside. You now know how to trace the connection, which is the whole point of this course.

Suryodaya Appliances is a fictional company created for this case study, and every figure in it is constructed for teaching. It is not a forecast, a model of any real business, or investment advice. Interest rates, exchange rates, multiples and outcomes were chosen to make the transmission chain arithmetically clear, and real situations involve many more variables. Nothing in this lesson is a recommendation regarding any security, and personal financial decisions should be taken with a qualified, registered adviser.
